title: How to Create The Perfect Set Of Class Rules https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2015/07/18/how-to-create-the-perfect-set-of-classroom-rules/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin offers a structured framework for writing effective classroom rules, arguing that rules should never be an afterthought or borrowed wholesale from a colleague. He specifies six criteria every rule must meet: simplicity, so students immediately understand the meaning; definability, so there's no gray area in what constitutes a violation; enforceability, ruling out vague sentiments like 'respect yourself'; expansiveness, so every possible misbehavior is covered by some rule; prominence, meaning rules should be posted boldly where they constantly remind students of their importance; and a focus on behavior only, kept separate from academic expectations like homework completion. He recommends a practical exercise of listing every misbehavior a teacher has witnessed and checking that each is covered by at least one rule, and offers his own four recommended rules as a proven starting point. The piece closes by pointing to SCM's broader archive for related guidance on modeling, routines, and first-day strategies.
points: Effective classroom rules must be simple, definable, enforceable, expansive, prominent, and focused on behavior only.
Vague rules like 'respect yourself' are unenforceable because they don't clearly define an observable violation.
Rules should be posted boldly and prominently to constantly remind students of their importance.
Academic expectations, like turning in homework, should never be mixed in with behavior rules.
A practical way to build a rule set is to list every misbehavior witnessed and verify each is covered by at least one rule.
quotes: They must be created thoughtfully and in a way that is relevant and meaningful to students.
Effective rules have no gray area. You must know without a doubt, and be able to communicate, exactly what is and isn’t okay.
It’s common for teachers to include rules that are virtually unenforceable. For example, ‘respect yourself’ is a nice sentiment, but too ambiguous to enforce.
If your rules aren’t important to you, then they won’t be important to your students. Place them high and bold on your classroom wall for the world to see.
Classroom rules must reflect behavior expectations only and kept separate from academic expectations.
The purpose of your rules is to protect yourself and your students from any and all misbehavior that disrupts learning. They act as an impenetrable wall, keeping interruptions out and inspiration in.
